proposal: The chapter recommends that Treasury work with Congress to replace the current individual income tax with two rates (15 percent and 30 percent), remove most deductions, credits and exclusions, cut the corporate rate to 18 percent, tax capital gains and qualified dividends at 15 percent, and allow immediate expensing. Over the longer term it favors a consumption-based tax (a national sales tax, business transfer tax, flat tax or cash-flow tax) and a three-fifths vote requirement to raise income or corporate rates.

status_summary: Public Law 119-21, signed 2025-07-04, made the 2017 individual rate schedules permanent rather than adopting a two-rate system: the IRS 2026 inflation-adjustment release of 2025-10-09 lists seven rates from 10 to 37 percent. The 21 percent corporate rate (set in 2017) was not changed by that law, and the enrolled law's table of contents has no section on the corporate rate. The Act did make 100 percent expensing of qualifying property permanent according to a law-firm summary, which overlaps with the chapter's expensing recommendation. No Treasury, White House or congressional proposal for the 15/30 structure, the 18 percent corporate rate, a consumption tax or a three-fifths vote requirement was found through October 2026.

timeline.event: Public Law 119-21 (H.R. 1) enacted. Section 70101 is titled as an extension and enhancement of reduced individual rates and Section 70102 as an extension and enhancement of the increased standard deduction (section titles from the table of contents of the enrolled text).

A law-firm summary reports that the 2017 income tax brackets were made permanent with a 37 percent top rate and that 100 percent bonus depreciation was made permanent (publication month August 2025; day set to the first of the month).

IRS release IR-2025-103 on tax year 2026 inflation adjustments lists seven individual rates (10, 12, 22, 24, 32, 35 and 37 percent), a 37 percent top rate, and a $32,200 standard deduction for joint filers.

title: Enact a two-rate individual income tax and an 18 percent corporate rate
uncertainties: The unchanged 21 percent corporate rate rests on the Cornell Legal Information Institute copy of 26 U.S.C. 11 (whose amendment notes may lag the 2025 law), the law's table of contents and summaries that list no change; I did not read the operative text of Title VII. The IRS release lists seven rates but does not itself say the rates were made permanent. Two searches for 2026 tax proposals (a second reconciliation package, a corporate rate cut, a flat tax) returned only 2025-era material, so the absence of a 2026 proposal for the 15/30 structure is a no-result finding, not a confirmation; Congress.gov could not be read. The choice of diverged over not_started is a judgment call.
